```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("R/clt_functions.R")
s <- read.csv("results/summary.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
s <- s[match(c("Normal(0,1)", "Six-sided die", "Exponential(1)", "Binomial(5, 0.1)", "Cauchy(0, 1)"), s$population), ]
get <- function(p, col) s[s$population == p, col]
repro <- read.csv("results/reproducibility.csv", check.names = FALSE)

real_keys  <- c("faithful", "discoveries", "diamonds", "flights", "counties")
real_names <- c("Old Faithful waiting times", "Great inventions per year", "Diamond prices",
                "NYC flight arrival delays", "Midwest county populations")
real_skew  <- c(skew(faithful$waiting), skew(as.numeric(discoveries)), skew(ggplot2::diamonds$price),
                skew(na.omit(nycflights13::flights$arr_delay)), skew(ggplot2::midwest$poptotal))
real <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(real_keys), function(i) {
  r <- read.csv(file.path("results", paste0("real_", real_keys[i], "_results.csv")))
  data.frame(name = real_names[i], skew = real_skew[i],
             n_pred = ceiling((real_skew[i] / 0.25)^2),
             n_main = smallest_normal_n(r),
             pass30 = r$normal_enough[r$n == 30])
}))
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## In plain words
Polls, drug trials and website experiments report results as "average ± margin". That margin is only right once the average
behaves like a bell curve, and statistics classes say 30 data points are enough for that. I simulated 100,000 studies
for every sample size, on textbook data and real data, to see how many points an average really needs. **The answer
depends on the data:** balanced data need fewer than 10, lopsided data like prices or delays need 50 to 2,450, and
some data never get there. New to the topic? Start with the [visual story](index.html).
:::

## Executive summary

I used Monte Carlo simulation in R (100,000 simulated samples for every sample size, seed 9426) to find
the smallest sample size n at which the sample mean is "normal enough" for five assigned populations,
and then for five real datasets. "Normal enough" means passing four calibrated checks (skewness, excess
kurtosis, Q-Q straightness, and the two tails of a 95% interval) and continuing to pass at every larger n.

1. **There is no universal n.** The answer ranged from **n = 1** (normal population) to
   **n = `r get("Binomial(5, 0.1)", "chosen_n")`** (rare-event binomial), and **no n at all** for the Cauchy.
2. **n = 30 is not a safe rule.** It is more than enough for symmetric populations, but too small for the
   skewed exponential (n = `r get("Exponential(1)", "chosen_n")`) and binomial, and for 4 of 5 real datasets.
3. **Skewness predicts the answer.** Because the skewness of the mean shrinks as skewness/√n, the threshold is
   about n ≈ (skewness / 0.25)². This predicted 64 for the exponential (simulated: `r get("Exponential(1)", "chosen_n")`) and
   came close for the continuous real datasets.
4. **Discreteness adds a separate delay.** The binomial passed the skewness check by n = 30 but needed
   n = `r get("Binomial(5, 0.1)", "chosen_n")` before its stair-step Q-Q plot and jumping tail rates settled.
5. **Infinite variance breaks the theorem.** For the Cauchy, the mean of 5,000 values has exactly the same
   spread as a single value. Large n does not help at all.
6. **The standard error formula σ/√n held at every n** for every population with finite variance, even
   where the shape was still far from normal. The shape is the slow part, not the spread.

## My standard for "normal enough"

| Check | Pass zone | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Skewness | \|skew\| ≤ 0.25 | keeps each tail of a 95% interval within about 0.7 points of 2.5% |
| Excess kurtosis | \|kurt\| ≤ 0.5 | about 10× the Monte Carlo noise; catches heavy tails |
| Q-Q correlation | r ≥ 0.998 | the Q-Q equivalent of skewness 0.25 |
| Tails | 1.75%–3.25% on **each** side | the practical goal itself, checked one side at a time |

The thresholds were calibrated by simulation (details in [Method](methods.qmd)). Every result is also
reported under a strict standard (skewness ≤ 0.1) and a lenient one (skewness ≤ 0.5).

```{r}
#| label: fig-summary
#| fig-cap: "Smallest n judged normal enough (main standard), with the strict–lenient range as a bar. The dashed line is the n = 30 rule of thumb."
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| echo: false
pops <- c("Normal", "Die", "Exponential", "Binomial", "Cauchy")
nm <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(s$chosen_n)); ns <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(s$n_strict)); nl <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(s$n_lenient))
style_par(mar = c(4.2, 7.5, 1, 1))
plot(NA, xlim = c(1, 5000), ylim = c(0.5, 5.5), log = "x", yaxt = "n", xlab = "Sample size n (log scale)", ylab = "")
axis(2, at = 5:1, labels = pops, las = 1, tick = FALSE)
abline(v = c(1, 10, 100, 1000), col = pal$grid)
abline(v = 30, lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = pal$ink)
for (i in 1:5) {
  y <- 6 - i
  if (is.na(nm[i])) {
    arrows(1, y, 5000, y, col = pal$fail, lwd = 3, length = 0.12)
    text(2000, y + 0.25, "never", col = pal$fail, font = 2)
  } else {
    segments(nl[i], y, ns[i], y, lwd = 8, col = adjustcolor(pal$bars, 0.3))
    points(nm[i], y, pch = 19, cex = 2, col = ifelse(nm[i] <= 30, pal$pass, pal$accent))
    text(nm[i], y + 0.3, nm[i], font = 2)
  }
}
text(30, 5.45, "n = 30", pos = 4, font = 2, cex = 0.9)
```

## Answers to the research questions

### Sample size: is there evidence for a universal rule such as n = 30?

**No.** The required n depends on the population and spans more than three orders of magnitude, and for one
population it does not exist. n = 30 happens to correspond roughly to my *lenient* standard: under that
standard every finite-variance population I tested passes by about n = 20 or less, except the heavy-tailed
real datasets. Under my main standard, which keeps each tail of a 95% interval within 0.75 points of 2.5%,
30 is too small for every strongly skewed population. So the rule of thumb is only safe if you accept one-sided
error rates that can be off by a factor of 1.5 to 2.5.

### Population shape: which converged fastest, which slowest, and why?

- **Fastest:** the normal (n = 1, already normal), then the die (n = `r get("Six-sided die", "chosen_n")`) and the Old
  Faithful waiting times (n = `r real$n_main[1]`). All are symmetric or nearly so, so their skewness is zero or small from the
  start, and mainly kurtosis and discreteness have to fade.
- **Slowest (finite variance):** the binomial (n = `r get("Binomial(5, 0.1)", "chosen_n")`) and exponential
  (n = `r get("Exponential(1)", "chosen_n")`) among the assigned populations; county populations (n = `r num(real$n_main[5])`)
  among the real data. The exponential is held back by skewness, the binomial by discreteness, and the county
  data by a few extreme values (skewness 12).
- **Never:** the Cauchy.

The main driver is the population's skewness, because the skewness of the mean decreases only as 1/√n:
halving the remaining skewness requires four times as much data. Kurtosis decreases as 1/n and was never the
limiting factor for finite-variance populations.

### Assumptions: what happened when they were violated?

- **Infinite variance (Cauchy):** the CLT does not apply at all. The interquartile range of the sample mean
  stayed at 2.0 from n = 1 to n = 5,000, and skewness and kurtosis estimates jumped randomly because the true
  values do not exist. The sample *median* does converge, so the right response to such data is a robust statistic.
- **Dependent observations** and **non-identically distributed observations** were offered as extra-credit
  extensions and are not part of this submission. The real-data page notes where independence is likely to
  fail in practice (flight delays on the same day are correlated).

## Reproducibility

Every simulation uses seed 9426, set immediately before each sample size, and B = 100,000. As required, I reran
the exponential analysis with a different seed:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-repro
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(repro, align = "r")
```

The exact numbers changed, but the conclusion did not: the threshold stayed in the same narrow range around
the theoretical 64, and n = 30 failed under both seeds. The seed makes the results **reproducible**; the large
B makes them **reliable**.

To reproduce everything: open `clt-monte-carlo.Rproj` in RStudio and run `quarto render`, then
`Rscript R/export_site_data.R` for the website data. Packages: knitr, rmarkdown, ggplot2, nycflights13, jsonlite.

## Limitations

- "Normal enough" is a judgment call. I report three standards so readers can apply their own.
- Near a threshold, Monte Carlo noise can flip a single n. The "keeps passing for every larger n" rule and
  B = 100,000 reduce but cannot remove this; answers should be read as ±5%.
- The strict and lenient answers use a coarser grid than the main answer, so they are approximate.
- The real datasets are treated as complete populations and sampled with replacement.
